title: CASE OF D.H. AND OTHERS v. THE CZECH REPUBLIC
summary: In the case of D.H. and Others v. the Czech Republic, the applicants were a group of children of Roma origin, representing the Roma and Travellers community, who brought a complaint against the Czech Republic. The heart of the case was the vulnerability of Roma children to systemic discrimination in education, specifically their disproportionate placement in special schools intended for pupils with learning disabilities. Between 1996 and 1999, the applicants were placed in such special schools in Ostrava, often following psychological assessments and with parental consent, though the applicants later argued that their parents had not been fully informed of the consequences. The applicants contended that this practice resulted in de facto segregation, as Roma children were overwhelmingly represented in these schools, which offered an inferior curriculum and limited future opportunities. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), but in its 2006 Chamber judgment, found no violation, concluding that the procedures had been followed and there was insufficient evidence of discrimination. This decision was significant as it highlighted the persistent challenges Roma and Travellers face in accessing equal education in Europe, reflecting a long history of segregation and marginalisation; the case would later be reconsidered by the Grand Chamber, marking a turning point in European anti-discrimination jurisprudence.
